dati_metodo: 1,666 first VC investments by 75 lead investors in CA and MA companies, 1982-1995 (SDC data); structural two-sided matching model estimated by Bayesian (Gibbs) methods; outcome is IPO

righe.estrazione: The abstract and introduction say sorting is almost twice as important as influence for the difference in IPO rates across VC investors. A worked example in Section F gives influence about one-third and sorting about two-thirds when moving from the least to the most experienced investor. The text says 'almost twice', not 'about twice', and the outcome is IPO, not exit in general.
righe.citazione: with sorting appearing almost twice as important as inf luence for explaining the observed differences in IPO rates across VC investors
righe.frase_paper: Sørensen (2007) finds that sorting of better companies to more experienced VCs is almost twice as important as the VCs' influence in explaining differences in IPO rates, in a sample of 1,666 first VC investments in California and Massachusetts, 1982-1995.
righe.frase_slide: Sorting is almost twice as important as influence for IPO-rate differences across VCs (Sørensen, 2007)
righe.numero_chiave: almost 2x: sorting vs influence in explaining IPO-rate differences across VC investors; roughly two-thirds sorting vs one-third influence for least vs most experienced investor
righe.limiti_vs_noi: Outcome is IPO only; CA and MA only; first investments 1982-1995; investor experience is the treatment, not the round gap; our setting is US 2012-2019 with exit within five years.
righe.note: Wording 'about twice' (v4) is slightly stronger than 'almost twice'; the 'per v4' part cannot be checked in this txt.

righe.estrazione: The paper separates two reasons why experienced VCs have more IPOs: influence (they add value) and sorting (they invest in better companies). It builds a structural matching model to identify the two. The tesi is a bare label and the txt covers it fully; the comparison of the two is only for IPO and VC experience.
righe.citazione: influence, which means that experienced VCs add more value and bring companies public at a higher rate, and sorting, which means that more experienced VCs invest in better companies
righe.frase_paper: Sørensen (2007) models the distinction between influence, where experienced VCs add value, and sorting, where they select better companies, and estimates both in a matching model.
righe.frase_slide: Better outcomes can reflect VC influence or selection of better companies (Sørensen, 2007)
righe.limiti_vs_noi: Treatment is investor experience, outcome is IPO, 1982-1995 CA and MA; no round gap or hype.
righe.note: Shared tesi with gompers2020: only the selection vs influence distinction is judged here for Sørensen.

righe.estrazione: Both effects are significant, but sorting is larger: almost twice as important as influence for IPO-rate differences. In the numerical decomposition sorting accounts for about two-thirds. The influence estimate is flagged as sensitive to the error structure. The claim holds for investor experience and IPO outcomes.
righe.citazione: Both effects are found to be significant, with sorting almost twice as important as inf luence for the difference in IPO rates.
righe.frase_paper: Sørensen (2007) finds that sorting of companies to more experienced VCs outweighs the VCs' influence in explaining differences in IPO rates.
righe.frase_slide: Sorting of better companies to experienced VCs outweighs influence on IPO rates (Sørensen, 2007)
righe.numero_chiave: almost 2x: sorting vs influence for IPO-rate differences
righe.limiti_vs_noi: IPO only; CA and MA, 1982-1995; experience of the lead investor, not funding gap.
righe.note: The tesi says 'better ventures to better investors'; the txt defines better investors as more experienced VCs.
